entry.evidence: There is a great paucity of data for the central transitional/translational domain of gravity collapse structures both offshore of SW Africa and worldwide

sequences.source_document: Publisher full text from XML (jats_text), checked against the published PDF

steps.action: Set the aim of examining the poorly imaged translational domain of a buried DWFTB system, its relation to the compressional domain, and its effect on younger deposits.
steps.quote: An examination of the translational domain in a buried DWFTB system is done in this study

steps.action: Used an industry 3D reflection seismic survey that Shell commissioned, acquired and processed (pre-stack depth migration); the authors interpreted the processed volume.
steps.quote: In this study we interpreted the processed seismic data obtained from Shell.

steps.action: Characterized the vertical and horizontal seismic resolution limits of the data from a reported average velocity and the dominant frequency.
steps.quote: the vertical seismic resolution limit given for the half and quarter dominant wavelength criteria (Yilmaz, 2001) is 60 and 30 m, respectively

steps.action: Conditioned the volume with structural smoothing and applied variance (volume) and edge-detection and influential-data (horizon) attributes in Petrel to delineate faults and erosional surfaces.
steps.quote: Using the structurally smoothed volume as input, the variance attribute was applied to enhance fault discontinuities throughout the seismic section.

steps.action: Picked nine key stratigraphic markers using seismic-stratigraphic criteria and assigned their ages by comparison with published Orange Basin studies and well data.
steps.quote: The geological ages used for stratigraphic markers in this study were postulated from the comparison of the aforementioned past studies and published well data.

steps.action: Estimated approximate sequence thicknesses through a generalized interval-velocity depth conversion, using velocities from shelf well logs reported by Kuhlmann et al. (2010).
steps.quote: a generalized depth conversion was carried out using average interval velocities from well logs acquired in the shallower reaches of the Orange Basin

steps.action: Described nine seismic sequences (A to D3), the Oligocene canyon, the Miocene slope-parallel channels, the seafloor slump above a B2 syncline, and the fault framework of the compressional and translational domains.
steps.quote: The surfaces are markers that divide the entire seismic succession into nine stratigraphic sequences

steps.action: Set Dalton et al.'s (2017) downward fault-propagation model for the small underlying DWFTBs against their own proposal that these structures are an older, separate gravitational collapse.
steps.quote: we propose the smaller, localized folds and thrusts observed below the main, kilometre-scale Late Cretaceous DWFTB system simply represent an older gravitational collapse system

steps.action: Dated the end of thrusting to the late Campanian from the C2 reflection configuration and compared this with de Vera et al. (2010) for the Namibian DWFTB system to the north.
steps.quote: This observation correlates with that of a DWFTB system observed directly north of the study area in the Namibian Orange Basin

steps.action: Interpreted the kinematics: renewed faulting along pre-existing weaknesses, oblique-slip faults post-dating thrusts, and en-echelon normal faults indicating lower tensional shear.
steps.quote: We interpret en-echelon-type and stair-stepped geometries of the small normal faults observed in the centre of the compressional domain

steps.action: Compared the oblique-slip framework and the unimaged extensional domain with analogous Orange Basin systems (de Vera et al. 2010; Scarselli et al. 2016) and the Niger Delta.
steps.quote: The outer oblique-slip faults described centrally in this study are analogous to the sidewall faults they described for each megaslide complex

steps.action: Stated two published rival views of the translational domain: an overprinted contact zone, or a fixed, mostly undeformed package marking a short-wavelength change.
steps.quote: There are two different schools of thought in what the translational domain represents

steps.action: Compared the observed width of the translational domain (more than about 20 km) with the narrow (~10 km) domain of previous Orange Basin interpretations.
steps.quote: what is observed is that the translational domain reaches and is greater than ∼ 20 km in width

steps.action: Proposed a third model: an overprinted zone marking a long-wavelength change, with downslope translation accommodated by extensive oblique-slip faults and internal strain redistribution.
steps.quote: We therefore propose a third model for what the translational domain represents

steps.action: Interpreted the Oligocene canyon as eroded by a downslope turbidity current and the Miocene margin-parallel channels as eroded by bottom currents, from orientation and geometry.
steps.quote: The Oligocene canyon is interpreted as having been formed by the erosive action of a turbidity current

steps.action: Rejected fault control of the canyon and channels, which the 2D section suggested, because in the 3D plan view they do not follow the trends of the underlying faults.
steps.quote: both the Oligocene canyon and Miocene channels do not appear to be influenced by the underlying tectonics

steps.action: Matched the 1200 to 1500 m depth range of the channels to published water-mass depths, attributing them to the AAIW-NADW interface and BUS intensification; cited a Namibian analogue.
steps.quote: the specific bottom water currents responsible for them are the upper northbound AAIW and deeper southbound NADW

steps.action: Tentatively proposed that the seafloor slump was triggered by AAIW/NADW currents above the weak syncline zone, possibly with fault reactivation below seismic resolution.
steps.quote: the seafloor slump scar observed in Fig. 7 may possibly have been triggered by the AAIW and NADW

steps.action: Assembled the observations and published ages into a six-stage temporal evolutionary model of the basin (Fig. 12).
steps.quote: we present a model in Fig. 12 illustrating the temporal evolution of the deep-water Orange Basin

steps.action: Kept the conclusions on the translational domain, the hindering of fault propagation by Cenozoic mass-flow deposits, and ocean-current control of mid-Cenozoic sedimentation.
steps.quote: The translational domain of is a zone containing overprinted features of both the extensional and compressional tectonics.

end.claim: The translational domain of the Orange Basin DWFTB system is a broad (more than about 20 km), long-wavelength zone of overprinted extensional and compressional features, with downslope translation accommodated by oblique-slip faults; mid-Cenozoic channels record the interface of the AAIW and NADW bottom currents.

decisive_move.sentence: Imaging the translational domain in 3D seismic data, with its normal, oblique-slip and thrust faults and its width of more than about 20 km, is what the third model rests on.

gates.evidence: Action: the data are an existing Shell industry survey, acquired and processed for exploration rather than directed by a stated hypothesis (§3 ¶1). Claim: the observed width of the translational domain could have matched the narrow (~10 km) domain of the rival view (§5.2.4 ¶2), and fault control of the canyon was checked in the 3D view (§5.3.1 ¶3); most other attributions rest on agreement with the literature. Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before interpretation.

imports.item: Gaussian-filter local averaging (structural smoothing) to raise signal-to-noise ratio
Edge-detection attribute that normalizes dip and azimuth to local noise

novelty_claims.quote: We therefore propose a third model for what the translational domain represents
the observations drawn add to the limited understanding of what occurs in the translational domains of passive margin settings

limits: No well log data were available, so interpretation is in the time domain. Depth conversion uses generic shelf velocities, and marker ages are borrowed from published frameworks, not dated here. The extensional domain is not imaged, so the true extent of the translational domain cannot be constrained (§5.2.4 ¶2). The paper gives two different dominant frequencies (50 Hz in §3.1 ¶1, ~20 Hz in §3.2.1 ¶1), so the stated resolution limits are uncertain. The authors note that basin-floor turbidites in the poorly imaged B1 sequence could be mistaken for small DWFTBs; they report 'careful inspection' but no test (§5.1.2 ¶1). Sub-claims at other statuses: the fault-geometry and stratigraphic descriptions are observational characterizations with no stated uncertainty; the canyon's link to a sea-level fall at ~30 Ma and the channels' attribution to the AAIW/NADW interface are best explanations drawn from cited oceanographic and sea-level literature; the slump trigger is speculative ('may possibly', §5.3.2 ¶4) and should be read as none; the older-collapse reading of the small DWFTBs is a proposal without a discriminating test. The review statement names three referees, but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Inference: the walk is interpretive and post hoc; the hypotheses appear after the data were in hand.
